## Appendix A Deterministic Amount Single-Goal Benchmarks

This appendix records the benchmarks used in Section 7.2 to validate the numerical solutions. These benchmarks correspond to the case where the goals are deterministic and the controls are unconstrained. They fall outside the standing assumptions of Section 3, which require a compact set of controls and rewards with continuous distributions, but have explicit solutions which provide intuition for the problem structure.

### A.1 Deterministic Deadline Goal

Fix $g>0$ and suppose $G\equiv g$ . The unconstrained fixed deadline benchmark is

$$ V^{D}_{\mathrm{Browne}}(t,w;g):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\geq g\}}\right],\qquad(t,w)\in[0,T)\times[0,\infty), $$

where the supremum is over admissible $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable portfolio rules without leverage or short-selling constraints that are locally square-integrable on $[t,T)$ . For this benchmark, terminal wealth is defined by the finite nonnegative limit $\widetilde{W}_{T}:=\lim_{s\uparrow T}\widetilde{W}_{s}$ . Note that if $w\geq g$ , the household can invest only in the money-market account and lock in success, so $V^{D}_{\mathrm{Browne}}(t,w;g)=1$ , while $V^{D}_{\mathrm{Browne}}(t,0;g)=0$ .

Define $\gamma^{2}:=\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{\theta}$ and assume $\gamma^{2}>0$ . The unconstrained solution in Browne (1999) is

$$ V^{D}_{\mathrm{Browne}}(t,w;g)=\Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{w}{g}\right)+\gamma\sqrt{T-t}\right),\qquad 0<w<g,\qquad 0\leq t<T, $$

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. An optimal feedback control is

$$ \bm{\pi}^{\ast}(t,w;g)=\frac{g}{w}\frac{\phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{w}{g}\right)\right)}{\gamma\sqrt{T-t}}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{\theta},\qquad 0<w<g,\qquad 0\leq t<T, $$

where $\phi$ is the standard normal density. This is locally square-integrable on $[t,T)$ and attains (34). Note that the portfolio fraction can become unbounded as $t\uparrow T$ , while terminal wealth remains well defined. Moreover, $\lim_{t\uparrow T}V^{D}_{\mathrm{Browne}}(t,w;g)=w/g$ for $0<w<g$ , so the unconstrained value does not, in fact, converge to the indicator payoff at the terminal boundary. The compact portfolio constraint in our main model rules out this gambling effect near the deadline and restores consistency with the boundary data in (18).

### A.2 Random Deadline Goal

Fix $c>0$ and suppose $R\equiv c$ , so $F_{R}(w)=\mathbf{1}_{\{w\geq c\}}$ . We consider a direct multi-asset extension of the single risky asset problem in Bayraktar and Young (2016) with no consumption. The unconstrained value is

$$ V^{R}_{\rm BY}(w):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{W}_{\tau}^{0,w;\bm{\pi}}\geq c\}}\right],\qquad w\geq 0, $$

where the supremum is again over admissible $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable portfolio rules without leverage or short-selling constraints that are locally square-integrable on $[0,\infty)$ . On smooth parts of the candidate value, the formal HJB is

$$ \lambda V^{R}_{\rm BY}(w)=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{w(V^{R}_{\rm BY})^{\prime}(w)\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}w^{2}(V^{R}_{\rm BY})^{\prime\prime}(w)\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}+\lambda F_{R}(w)\right\}. $$

On $0<w<c$ , a power candidate gives

$$ V^{R}_{\rm BY}(w)=\left(\frac{w}{c}\right)^{\kappa},\qquad\bm{\pi}_{\rm BY}^{*}=\frac{1}{1-\kappa}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{\theta},\qquad\kappa=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\tfrac{1}{2}\gamma^{2}}. $$

The verification argument of Bayraktar and Young (2016) yields

$$ V^{R}_{\rm BY}(w)=\begin{cases}(w/c)^{\kappa},&0\leq w<c,\\[3.0pt]
1,&w\geq c.\end{cases} $$

If $\Pi_{K}$ contains both $0$ and $\bm{\pi}_{\rm BY}^{*}$ , the constrained value equals this benchmark. Indeed, one can use $\bm{\pi}_{\rm BY}^{*}$ until wealth reaches $c$ and the zero strategy thereafter. This policy is both feasible for the constrained problem and attains the unconstrained value.

## Appendix B Viscosity Proofs

### B.1 Deterministic Deadline Goal

As in Section 3, fix the nonempty compact set $\Pi_{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ containing $0$ , and write

$$ H(w,p,q):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{wp\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}w^{2}q\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}\right\}. $$

We write the HJB equation appearing in (17) either as

$$ u_{t}+H(w,u_{w},u_{ww})=0 $$

or, equivalently, in terms of $\mathcal{F}_{D}(t,w,z,a,p,q):=-a-H(w,p,q)$ .

Here $z$ is the value variable. It is included only to match standard viscosity notation since the fixed-deadline equation has no zero-order term.

A viscosity subsolution of $\mathcal{F}_{D}=0$ satisfies $\mathcal{F}_{D}\leq 0$ . Thus, if a smooth test function $\phi$ touches a subsolution from above at $(t,w)$ , then

$$ -\phi_{t}(t,w)-H(w,\phi_{w}(t,w),\phi_{ww}(t,w))\leq 0, $$

equivalently $\phi_{t}+H\geq 0$ . A viscosity supersolution satisfies the reverse inequality. This is the sign convention used throughout the proof below. We begin with a preliminary result about $H$ .

#### Lemma B.1.

For fixed $\Pi_{K}$ , the Hamiltonian $H$ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Moreover, on every compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , $H$ is Lipschitz. Finally, if $q_{1}\leq q_{2}$ , then $H(w,p,q_{1})\leq H(w,p,q_{2})$ for all $(w,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . Consequently, $\mathcal{F}_{D}$ is continuous, proper, and degenerate elliptic.

#### Proof.

For $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , define $\mathfrak{g}(w,p,q;\bm{\pi}):=w\,p\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,w^{2}\,q\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{\pi}$ . Fix a compact set $C\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Because $\Pi_{K}$ is compact, there is a constant $M_{K}<\infty$ such that $\|\bm{\pi}\|\leq M_{K}$ for every $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ . Since $\mathfrak{g}$ is polynomial in $(w,p,q,\bm{\pi})$ , there exists $L_{C,K}<\infty$ with

$$ |\mathfrak{g}(\xi;\bm{\pi})-\mathfrak{g}(\eta;\bm{\pi})|\leq L_{C,K}\,\|\xi-\eta\|\qquad\text{for all }\xi,\eta\in C,\ \bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}. $$

Taking the supremum over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ yields $|H(\xi)-H(\eta)|\leq L_{C,K}\,\|\xi-\eta\|$ for $\xi,\eta\in C$ , so $H$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz.

If $q_{1}\leq q_{2}$ , then for every $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , $\mathfrak{g}(w,p,q_{1};\bm{\pi})\leq\mathfrak{g}(w,p,q_{2};\bm{\pi})$ because $\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\,\bm{\pi}\geq 0$ . Taking suprema gives $H(w,p,q_{1})\leq H(w,p,q_{2})$ . Therefore $\mathcal{F}_{D}$ is nonincreasing in $q$ , i.e. degenerate elliptic. It is proper because it is independent of the value variable (therefore nondecreasing), and it is continuous by the continuity of $H$ . ∎

We note that since the control set $\Pi_{K}$ is compact, the drift and diffusion coefficients for the wealth $b(w,\bm{\pi})=w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}$ , $\sigma_{W}(w,\bm{\pi})=w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}$ are globally Lipschitz in $w$ with constants uniform in $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , and satisfy a uniform linear-growth bound. Hence, for every admissible control, the wealth equation has a unique strong solution and the problem is well-posed.

#### Lemma B.2.

The value function $V^{D}(t,w)$ is jointly continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ .

#### Proof.

The continuous function $F_{G}$ is constant outside $[0,b_{G}]$ and hence uniformly continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ . Choose Lipschitz functions $F_{G}^{m}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ such that

$$ F_{G}^{m}(x)=0\quad\text{for }x\leq 0,\qquad F_{G}^{m}(x)=1\quad\text{for }x\geq b_{G},\qquad\|F_{G}^{m}-F_{G}\|_{\infty}\to 0. $$

For instance, one may take the piecewise-linear approximations of $F_{G}$ on partitions of $[0,b_{G}]$ and extend them continuously to constant values outside of this interval.

For each $m$ , define the auxiliary value function

$$ V_{m}(t,w):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{t,T}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{G}^{m}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right],\qquad(t,w)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}. $$

Observe that we have extended the domain to all of $\mathbb{R}$ but this does not pose a problem since the wealth SDE is still well-posed and clearly $V_{m}(t,w)=0$ if $w\leq 0$ . For fixed $m$ , this is a finite-horizon stochastic control problem in Mayer form with bounded control set $\Pi_{K}$ , Lipschitz terminal payoff $F_{G}^{m}$ , and coefficients that have linear growth in $(w,\pi)$ and are Lipschitz in the state uniformly over the controls. Therefore (Touzi, 2013, Proposition 3.7) applies and gives $V_{m}\in C([0,T]\times\mathbb{R})$ . More precisely, $V_{m}$ is Lipschitz in the wealth variable, uniformly in time, and $1/2$ -Hölder continuous in time on compact wealth intervals.

We now compare $V_{m}$ with $V^{D}$ . For every $(t,w)\in[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|V_{m}(t,w)-V^{D}(t,w)\right| \displaystyle\leq\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{t,T}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|F_{G}^{m}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)-F_{G}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right|\right]\leq\|F_{G}^{m}-F_{G}\|_{\infty}. $$

Thus $V_{m}\to V^{D}$ uniformly on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ . Since each $V_{m}$ is continuous, the uniform limit $V^{D}$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ . ∎

Our next result gives the usual comparison principle for viscosity solutions. For an open domain $Q\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , we write $USC(\overline{Q})$ and $LSC(\overline{Q})$ for the classes of real-valued functions on $\overline{Q}$ that are upper and lower semicontinuous relative to $\overline{Q}$ , respectively.

#### Lemma B.3 (Comparison).

Let $Q:=(0,T)\times(0,b_{G})$ , and let $u\in USC(\overline{Q})$ and $v\in LSC(\overline{Q})$ be bounded. Suppose that $u$ is a viscosity subsolution and $v$ is a viscosity supersolution of

$$ -u_{t}-H(w,u_{w},u_{ww})=0\qquad\text{in }Q. $$

Assume further that the parabolic boundary inequalities

$$ u(T,w)\leq F_{G}(w)\leq v(T,w),\qquad 0\leq w\leq b_{G}, $$

and

$$ u(t,0)\leq 0\leq v(t,0),\qquad u(t,b_{G})\leq 1\leq v(t,b_{G}),\qquad 0\leq t\leq T, $$

hold. Then $u\leq v$ on $(0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ .

#### Proof.

We reduce the statement to the Cauchy–Dirichlet comparison theorem of (Crandall et al., 1992, Theorem 8.2). Set $s:=T-t$ , $h(w):=\frac{w}{b_{G}}$ , and define

$$ U(s,w):=u(T-s,w)-h(w),\qquad V(s,w):=v(T-s,w)-h(w),\qquad(s,w)\in[0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]. $$

Then $U\in USC([0,T]\times[0,b_{G}])$ and $V\in LSC([0,T]\times[0,b_{G}])$ . The time reversal turns the terminal condition into an initial condition, and the subtraction of $h$ (which is introduced to match the boundary conditions) makes it so

$$ U(0,w)\leq F_{G}(w)-h(w)\leq V(0,w),\qquad 0\leq w\leq b_{G}, $$

and $U(s,0)\leq 0\leq V(s,0)$ , $U(s,b_{G})\leq 0\leq V(s,b_{G})$ , for $0\leq s\leq T$ .

We now identify the transformed equation. If $\psi$ is a smooth test function for $U$ , then the corresponding test function for $u$ is $\phi(t,w):=\psi(T-t,w)+h(w)$ . Thus

$$ \phi_{t}(t,w)=-\psi_{s}(T-t,w),\qquad\phi_{w}(t,w)=\psi_{w}(T-t,w)+h^{\prime}(w),\qquad\phi_{ww}(t,w)=\psi_{ww}(T-t,w)+h^{\prime\prime}(w). $$

Since $h^{\prime}(w)=1/b_{G}$ and $h^{\prime\prime}(w)=0$ , the viscosity inequalities for $u$ and $v$ transform into the viscosity inequalities for $U$ and $V$ associated with $z_{s}+F_{h}(w,z_{w},z_{ww})=0$ in $(0,T)\times(0,b_{G})$ , where

$$ F_{h}(w,p,q):=-H\left(w,p+\frac{1}{b_{G}},q\right). $$

Hence $U$ is a viscosity subsolution and $V$ is a viscosity supersolution of this Cauchy–Dirichlet problem with continuous initial data $F_{G}-h$ . This is precisely the problem in (Crandall et al., 1992, Equation (8.4)).

It remains to verify the structural assumptions needed for (Crandall et al., 1992, Theorem 8.2). By Lemma B.1, the operator $F_{h}$ is continuous, and it is proper because it is independent of the value variable and is degenerate elliptic: if $q_{1}\leq q_{2}$ , then $H(w,p,q_{1})\leq H(w,p,q_{2})$ , and therefore $F_{h}(w,p,q_{1})\geq F_{h}(w,p,q_{2})$ .

Lastly, the structural condition (Crandall et al., 1992, Equation (3.14)) holds by a direct application of (Crandall et al., 1992, Example 3.6). Indeed, for each $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ define

$$ b^{\bm{\pi}}(w):=-w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta},\qquad Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w):=\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}\bigr)^{1/2},\qquad f^{\bm{\pi}}(w):=\frac{w}{b_{G}}\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}. $$

Then, identifying $Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)$ with a $1\times 1$ matrix,

$$ F_{h}(w,p,q)=\inf_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{b^{\bm{\pi}}(w)p-\operatorname{tr}\!\left(Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)^{\top}Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)q\right)-f^{\bm{\pi}}(w)\right\}. $$

For each fixed $\bm{\pi}$ , this is a sum of the first-order, second-order, and continuous spatial terms covered by Example 3.6. Moreover, because $\Pi_{K}$ is compact, the one-sided Lipschitz constants for $b^{\bm{\pi}}$ , the Lipschitz constants for $Z^{\bm{\pi}}$ , and the moduli of continuity of $f^{\bm{\pi}}$ can be chosen uniformly over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ . The final stability statement in (Crandall et al., 1992, Example 3.6) therefore implies that the infimum over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ satisfies the same structural condition.

The Cauchy–Dirichlet comparison theorem (Crandall et al., 1992, Theorem 8.2) yields $U(s,w)\leq V(s,w)$ for all $(s,w)\in[0,T)\times[0,b_{G}]$ . Since $U-V=u(T-s,w)-v(T-s,w)$ , returning to the original variables gives $u\leq v$ on $(0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ . ∎

With these preliminaries, we complete the proof of the fixed-deadline part of Proposition 4.1.

#### Proof of the fixed-deadline part of Proposition 4.1.

We divide the proof into parts.

Step 1: (Regularity and Boundary Values) The value function is bounded because $0\leq F_{G}\leq 1$ and it is continuous by Lemma B.2. The boundary values are immediate. If $w=0$ , then wealth remains zero and $V^{D}(t,0)=F_{G}(0)=0$ . If $w=b_{G}$ , the household can choose $\bm{\pi}\equiv 0$ and lock in terminal wealth $b_{G}$ , so $V^{D}(t,b_{G})=1$ . At $t=T$ , no time remains to trade, and therefore $V^{D}(T,w)=F_{G}(w)$ .

Step 2: (Viscosity Solution) We note as in Lemma B.2 that the definition of $V^{D}$ readily extends to $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}$ with the same properties. Moreover, the present bounded-control Mayer problem falls within the stochastic-control framework of (Touzi, 2013, Section 7). Since $V^{D}$ is bounded and $H$ is finite and continuous, we may apply (Touzi, 2013, Theorem 7.4) to obtain that $V^{D}$ is a viscosity solution of (17) on $[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}$ and hence also on $[0,T)\times(0,b_{G})$ .

Step 3: (Uniqueness) Let $u$ and $v$ be two bounded continuous viscosity solutions of the equation $-u_{t}-H(w,u_{w},u_{ww})=0$ in $(0,T)\times(0,b_{G})$ , with the stated boundary data. Applying Lemma B.3 to $u$ as subsolution and $v$ as supersolution gives $u\leq v$ . Reversing the roles of $u$ and $v$ gives $v\leq u$ . Hence $u=v$ on $(0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ . This equality extends to $t=0$ by continuity. ∎

### B.2 Random Deadline Goal

Define $\mathcal{F}_{R}(w,z,p,q):=\lambda z-H(w,p,q)-\lambda F_{R}(w)$ , so that (19) is

$$ \mathcal{F}_{R}\bigl(w,V^{R}(w),(V^{R})^{\prime}(w),(V^{R})^{\prime\prime}(w)\bigr)=0. $$

Because the same clipped Hamiltonian $H$ appears here as in the fixed-deadline problem, Lemma B.1 implies that $H$ is finite and continuous, locally Lipschitz on compact sets, and nondecreasing in its second-derivative argument. Since $F_{R}$ is continuous, $\mathcal{F}_{R}$ is continuous. Moreover, $\mathcal{F}_{R}$ is strictly increasing in the value variable $z$ , with slope $\lambda>0$ , and is nonincreasing in the second-derivative argument $q$ . Hence $\mathcal{F}_{R}$ is proper and degenerate elliptic.

Our first supporting result proves the continuity of the value function $V^{R}$ .

#### Lemma B.4.

The value function $V^{R}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $F_{R}$ is continuous and constant outside $[0,b_{R}]$ , it is uniformly continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ . Let $\omega_{R}$ be a modulus of continuity for $F_{R}$ . Fix $N>0$ and define the truncated value

$$ V_{N}^{R}(w):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{0,\infty}}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{N}\lambda e^{-\lambda s}F_{R}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\,ds\right]. $$

The tail is uniformly bounded by

$$ 0\leq V^{R}(w)-V_{N}^{R}(w)\leq\int_{N}^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda s}\,ds=e^{-\lambda N}. $$

Hence, for $w,w^{\prime}\geq 0$ , $|V^{R}(w)-V^{R}(w^{\prime})|\leq|V_{N}^{R}(w)-V_{N}^{R}(w^{\prime})|+2e^{-\lambda N}$ .

We now prove continuity of $V_{N}^{R}$ . Couple the wealth processes started from $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ using the same Brownian motion and the same control $\bm{\pi}$ . Since $\Pi_{K}$ is bounded, the coefficients $b(x,\bm{\pi})=x\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}$ , $\sigma_{W}(x,\bm{\pi})=x\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}$ are globally Lipschitz in $x$ , uniformly over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , and have linear growth. Therefore the finite-horizon flow estimate of (Touzi, 2013, Theorem 2.4) gives, for each $N<\infty$ , a constant $C_{N,K}<\infty$ such that

$$ \sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{0,\infty}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq N}\left|\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w;\bm{\pi}}-\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w^{\prime};\bm{\pi}}\right|^{2}\right]\leq C_{N,K}|w-w^{\prime}|^{2}. $$

Consequently, for every $\eta>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|V_{N}^{R}(w)-V_{N}^{R}(w^{\prime})| \displaystyle\leq\sup_{\bm{\pi}}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{N}\lambda e^{-\lambda s}\left|F_{R}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)-F_{R}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w^{\prime};\bm{\pi}}\right)\right|ds\right] \displaystyle\leq\omega_{R}(\eta)+2\sup_{\bm{\pi}}\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq N}\left|\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w;\bm{\pi}}-\widetilde{W}_{s}^{0,w^{\prime};\bm{\pi}}\right|>\eta\right) \displaystyle\leq\omega_{R}(\eta)+\frac{2C_{N,K}}{\eta^{2}}|w-w^{\prime}|^{2}. $$

Letting $w^{\prime}\to w$ gives $\limsup_{w^{\prime}\to w}|V_{N}^{R}(w)-V_{N}^{R}(w^{\prime})|\leq\omega_{R}(\eta)$ . Then $\eta\downarrow 0$ proves continuity of $V_{N}^{R}$ . Finally, $\limsup_{w^{\prime}\to w}|V^{R}(w)-V^{R}(w^{\prime})|\leq 2e^{-\lambda N}$ , and letting $N\to\infty$ proves continuity of $V^{R}$ . ∎

Next, we prove the comparison principle for viscosity solutions of this elliptic problem.

#### Lemma B.5 (Comparison).

Let $\Omega_{R}:=(0,b_{R})$ . Suppose $u\in USC(\overline{\Omega}_{R})$ and $v\in LSC(\overline{\Omega}_{R})$ are bounded, $u$ is a viscosity subsolution and $v$ is a viscosity supersolution of

$$ \mathcal{F}_{R}(w,u,u^{\prime},u^{\prime\prime})=0\qquad\text{in }\Omega_{R}, $$

and $u(0)\leq v(0)$ , $u(b_{R})\leq v(b_{R})$ . Then $u\leq v$ on $\overline{\Omega}_{R}$ .

#### Proof.

We verify the hypotheses of (Crandall et al., 1992, Theorem 3.3). The domain $\Omega_{R}$ is bounded, and as noted above $\mathcal{F}_{R}$ is continuous and proper. Moreover, for $r>s$ ,

$$ \mathcal{F}_{R}(w,r,p,q)-\mathcal{F}_{R}(w,s,p,q)=\lambda(r-s), $$

so the condition in (Crandall et al., 1992, Equation (3.13)) holds with $\gamma=\lambda$ .

It remains only to verify the structural condition (Crandall et al., 1992, Equation (3.14)). We write

$$ \mathcal{F}_{R}(w,r,p,q)=\lambda r+\inf_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{-wp\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}-\frac{1}{2}w^{2}q\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}-\lambda F_{R}(w)\right\}. $$

For each $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , set $b^{\bm{\pi}}(w):=-w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}$ and $Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w):=\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}\bigr)^{1/2}$ . Then the controlled part has the form

$$ b^{\bm{\pi}}(w)p-\operatorname{tr}\left(Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)^{\top}Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)q\right)-\lambda F_{R}(w). $$

The first-order coefficients $b^{\bm{\pi}}$ are one-sided Lipschitz in $w$ uniformly over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , the diffusion factors $Z^{\bm{\pi}}$ are Lipschitz in $w$ uniformly over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , and the spatial term $\lambda F_{R}(w)$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,b_{R}]$ . Therefore (Crandall et al., 1992, Example 3.6) gives the structural condition with a common modulus, and this condition is preserved under the infimum over the compact control set $\Pi_{K}$ .

The comparison theorem yields $u\leq v$ in $\Omega_{R}$ . The boundary inequality gives the result on $\overline{\Omega}_{R}$ . ∎

We now turn to the proof of the random-deadline part of Proposition 4.1.

#### Proof of the random-deadline part of Proposition 4.1.

We once again divide the proof into parts.

Step 1: (Regularity and Boundary Values) The value is bounded between $0$ and $1$ since $0\leq F_{R}\leq 1$ and continuity follows from Lemma B.4. The boundary values are also immediate as before with $V^{D}$ . If $w=0$ , wealth remains zero and $F_{R}(0)=0$ , so $V^{R}(0)=0$ . If $w\geq b_{R}$ , the household can choose $\bm{\pi}\equiv 0$ , keeping wealth at least $b_{R}$ forever, and hence $V^{R}(w)=1$ .

Step 2: (Viscosity Solution) To see that the value function $V^{R}$ is a viscosity solution of

$$ \lambda u(w)-H\bigl(w,u^{\prime}(w),u^{\prime\prime}(w)\bigr)-\lambda F_{R}(w)=0\qquad\text{on }(0,b_{R}) $$

we view the random-deadline problem as an infinite-horizon discounted stochastic control problem, in the framework of (Pham, 2009, Section 4.3). To match the Euclidean-state formulation in (Pham, 2009, Section 4.3), we use the harmless extension of the coefficients and payoff to all $w\in\mathbb{R}$ . The state dynamics are autonomous:

$$ d\widetilde{W}_{t}=\widetilde{W}_{t}\left(\bm{\pi}_{t}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,dt+\bm{\pi}_{t}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dB_{t}\right),\qquad\bm{\pi}_{t}\in\Pi_{K} $$

and the control set is compact. Starting from $w>0$ , the solution remains strictly positive. The coefficients are continuous, globally Lipschitz in the state uniformly over $\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}$ , and satisfy a linear-growth bound. The running reward is $f(w,\bm{\pi}):=\lambda F_{R}(w)$ , which is bounded and continuous, and the discount rate is $\lambda>0$ .

In the notation of Pham (2009), the Hamiltonian is

$$ \widehat{H}(w,p,q):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{wp\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}w^{2}q\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}+\lambda F_{R}(w)\right\}=H(w,p,q)+\lambda F_{R}(w). $$

Since $\Pi_{K}$ is compact, $\widehat{H}$ is finite and continuous. Hence we are in the regular compact-control case55 5 We note that the infinite-horizon viscosity result is stated under the condition that (in our notation) $\lambda$ is “sufficiently large.” That condition is used in (Pham, 2009, Proposition 4.3.1) to ensure that the infinite-horizon payoff is well-defined in the unbounded reward setting, and to ensure that constant controls are admissible (see the invocation of (Pham, 2009, Remark 3.2.2) in the proof). In the present problem these requirements hold for every $\lambda>0$ , because the running reward is uniformly bounded over the admissible controls $\bm{\pi}$ and so we can dispense with this requirement. of (Pham, 2009, Theorem 4.3.1 and Remark 4.3.4) and the variational inequality reduces to the ordinary HJB equation. The argument in (Pham, 2009, Section 4.3 and Theorem 4.3.1) therefore applies in the present setting and gives that $V^{R}$ is a viscosity solution of

$$ \lambda V^{R}(w)-\widehat{H}\bigl(w,(V^{R})^{\prime}(w),(V^{R})^{\prime\prime}(w)\bigr)=0 $$

on $\mathbb{R}$ and hence, also on $(0,b_{R})$ . Substituting the expression for $\widehat{H}$ gives

$$ \lambda V^{R}(w)-H\bigl(w,(V^{R})^{\prime}(w),(V^{R})^{\prime\prime}(w)\bigr)-\lambda F_{R}(w)=0 $$

in the viscosity sense on $(0,b_{R})$ as required.

Step 3: (Uniqueness) Let $u$ and $v$ be two bounded continuous viscosity solutions of (19) on $(0,b_{R})$ with boundary values $u(0)=v(0)=0$ and $u(b_{R})=v(b_{R})=1$ . Applying Lemma B.5 first to $u$ as subsolution and $v$ as supersolution gives $u\leq v$ . Reversing the roles gives $v\leq u$ . Hence $u=v$ on $[0,b_{R}]$ . ∎

### B.3 Joint-Goal Problem

The two funding rules give the same HJB equation (26) and differ only in the terminal condition. As a result, we prove our main characterization result in terms of a general continuous terminal payoff $\Psi$ and apply it with $\Psi=\mathcal{T}$ and $\Psi=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ to prove Theorem 5.2 and Proposition 6.1.

Recall $b=b_{R}+b_{G}$ . Extend $\mathcal{J}$ to all real wealth by setting $\mathcal{J}(t,w)=0$ for $w\leq 0$ . Its definition gives $\mathcal{J}(t,w)=1$ for $w\geq b$ . Extend $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ in the same way, by zero on $(-\infty,0]$ and by one on $[b,\infty)$ .

#### Lemma B.6.

The running operator $\mathcal{J}$ belongs to $C([0,T]\times\mathbb{R})$ , and both terminal operators $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ belong to $C(\mathbb{R})$ . Moreover, all three functions take values in $[0,1]$ and are constant outside the compact wealth interval $[0,b]$ .

#### Proof.

Boundedness and the stated constant extensions follow from $0\leq V^{D},V^{R}\leq 1$ , $\alpha_{R}+\alpha_{D}=1$ , and the facts that $R\leq b_{R}$ and $G\leq b_{G}$ almost surely.

We first prove continuity of $\mathcal{J}$ on $[0,T]\times[0,b]$ . Let $(t_{m},w_{m})\to(t,w)$ in $[0,T]\times[0,b]$ . For every realization $r\neq w$ ,

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\{w_{m}\geq r\}}\longrightarrow\mathbf{1}_{\{w\geq r\}},\qquad w_{m}-r\mathbf{1}_{\{w_{m}\geq r\}}\longrightarrow w-r\mathbf{1}_{\{w\geq r\}}. $$

The continuity of $F_{R}$ gives $\mathbb{P}(R=w)=0$ , while Proposition 4.1 gives the joint continuity of $V^{D}$ . Dominated convergence in (21) therefore proves $\mathcal{J}(t_{m},w_{m})\to\mathcal{J}(t,w)$ .

The operator $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ is handled identically, using the continuity of $F_{G}$ and Proposition 4.1. For $\mathcal{T}$ , for every $g\neq w$ the feasible set $\Theta(w_{m},g)$ is eventually equal to $\Theta(w,g)$ , and the two candidate payoffs in (24) converge by continuity of $V^{R}$ . The maximum therefore converges pointwise for $G\neq w$ . Since, once again, $\mathbb{P}(G=w)=0$ and the maximum is bounded, dominated convergence proves continuity of $\mathcal{T}$ . ∎

We now introduce a general class of terminal data that includes $\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ by Lemma B.6.

#### Definition B.7 (Admissible terminal data).

Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be the class of continuous functions $\Psi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\Psi(w)=0$ for $w\leq 0$ , $\Psi(w)=1$ for $w\geq b$ .

For $\Psi\in\mathfrak{T}$ , define

$$ \widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(t,w):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{t,T}}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\mathcal{J}\!\left(s,\widetilde{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\,ds+e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\Psi\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right], $$

for $(t,w)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}$ , with the convention $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(T,w)=\Psi(w)$ . The multiplicative wealth equation is well posed for arbitrary real initial wealth. If $w\leq 0$ , its solution remains nonpositive, so the extensions above give $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(t,w)=0$ .

#### Lemma B.8.

For every $\Psi\in\mathfrak{T}$ , the value function $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}$ is continuous and $[0,1]$ -valued on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}$ .

#### Proof.

The range follows from $0\leq\mathcal{J},\Psi\leq 1$ and

$$ \int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\,ds+e^{-\lambda(T-t)}=1. $$

By Lemma B.6 and Definition B.7, $\mathcal{J}$ and $\Psi$ are uniformly continuous after their constant extensions. Choose bounded Lipschitz functions $\mathcal{J}_{m}:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ , $\Psi_{m}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ such that

$$ \varepsilon_{m}:=\|\mathcal{J}_{m}-\mathcal{J}\|_{\infty}+\|\Psi_{m}-\Psi\|_{\infty}\longrightarrow 0. $$

Let $V_{m}$ be the value in (38) with $(\mathcal{J}_{m},\Psi_{m})$ in place of $(\mathcal{J},\Psi)$ . Direct comparison of the payoffs gives

$$ \|V_{m}-\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{m}. $$

It remains to show that each $V_{m}$ is continuous as the uniform convergence in (39) would imply the continuity of $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}$ . The coefficients $\beta(w,\bm{\pi})=w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}$ , $\sigma_{W}(w,\bm{\pi})=w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}$ are Lipschitz in $w$ , uniformly over the compact set $\Pi_{K}$ , and have uniform linear growth. To put the running-payoff problem in the Mayer form used in (Touzi, 2013, Proposition 3.7) we may use the standard augmentation described in (Touzi, 2013, Remark 3.2(iii)). Take a bounded Lipschitz function $\chi$ that agrees with the identity on $[e^{-\lambda T},1]$ and augment the state by

$$ dY_{s}=\chi(Z_{s})\lambda\mathcal{J}_{m}(s,\widetilde{W}_{s})\,ds,\quad Y_{t}=0,\qquad dZ_{s}=-\lambda Z_{s}\,ds,\quad Z_{t}=1. $$

Then $Z_{s}=e^{-\lambda(s-t)}$ and the payoff is $Y_{T}+\chi(Z_{T})\Psi_{m}(\widetilde{W}_{T})$ , a Lipschitz function of the terminal augmented state. The augmented coefficients are Lipschitz in the state uniformly over $\Pi_{K}$ and have linear growth. Hence (Touzi, 2013, Proposition 3.7) gives $V_{m}\in C([0,T]\times\mathbb{R})$ . ∎

For $\Psi\in\mathfrak{T}$ , consider

$$ \partial_{t}u+H(w,u_{w},u_{ww})+\lambda\bigl(\mathcal{J}(t,w)-u\bigr)=0\quad\text{on }\Omega_{RD}:=(0,T)\times(0,b), $$

with boundary data

$$ u(T,w)=\Psi(w),\quad 0\leq w\leq b,\qquad u(t,0)=0,\quad u(t,b)=1,\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

#### Lemma B.9 (Comparison).

Fix $\Psi\in\mathfrak{T}$ . Let $u\in USC(\overline{\Omega}_{RD})$ , $v\in LSC(\overline{\Omega}_{RD})$ be bounded and suppose that $u$ is a viscosity subsolution and $v$ is a viscosity supersolution of (40) on $\Omega_{RD}$ . Assume further that

$$ u(T,w)\leq\Psi(w)\leq v(T,w),\qquad 0\leq w\leq b, $$

and $u(t,0)\leq 0\leq v(t,0)$ , $u(t,b)\leq 1\leq v(t,b)$ for $0\leq t\leq T$ . Then $u\leq v$ on $(0,T]\times[0,b]$ . If, in addition, $u$ and $v$ are continuous on $\overline{\Omega}_{RD}$ , the inequality also holds at $t=0$ .

#### Proof.

Set $s=T-t$ , $h(w)=w/b$ , and $U(s,w):=u(T-s,w)-h(w)$ , $V(s,w):=v(T-s,w)-h(w)$ . As before, $h$ is used to make the lateral boundary data homogeneous:

$$ U(s,0)\leq 0\leq V(s,0),\qquad U(s,b)\leq 0\leq V(s,b),\qquad 0\leq s\leq T. $$

The terminal inequalities become $U(0,w)\leq\Psi(w)-h(w)\leq V(0,w)$ for $0\leq w\leq b$ and the transformed operator is

$$ \widehat{F}(s,w,r,p,q):=\lambda\bigl(r+h(w)\bigr)-H\!\left(w,p+\frac{1}{b},q\right)-\lambda\mathcal{J}(T-s,w). $$

Thus $U$ and $V$ are respectively a viscosity subsolution and supersolution of $z_{s}+\widehat{F}(s,w,z,z_{w},z_{ww})=0$ on $(0,T)\times(0,b)$ , with the required initial and lateral boundary ordering.

The operator $\widehat{F}$ is continuous by Lemma B.1 and Lemma B.6. It is proper, with strictly positive slope $\lambda$ in the value variable, and is degenerate elliptic because $H$ is nondecreasing in $q$ . To verify (Crandall et al., 1992, Equation (3.14)), write

$$ \widehat{F}(s,w,r,p,q)=\lambda r+\inf_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{-\beta^{\bm{\pi}}(w)p-\bigl(Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)\bigr)^{2}q-f^{\bm{\pi}}(w)\right\}+\lambda h(w)-\lambda\mathcal{J}(T-s,w), $$

where

$$ \beta^{\bm{\pi}}(w)=w\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta},\qquad Z^{\bm{\pi}}(w)=\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}\bigr)^{1/2},\qquad f^{\bm{\pi}}(w)=\frac{w}{b}\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}. $$

Because $\Pi_{K}$ is compact, the Lipschitz constants of these coefficients can be chosen uniformly in $\bm{\pi}$ . The remaining spatial term is uniformly continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,b]$ . Consequently (Crandall et al., 1992, Example 3.6) supplies the structural condition with a common modulus, and the infimum over $\Pi_{K}$ preserves it. The comparison theorem (Crandall et al., 1992, Theorem 8.2) gives $U\leq V$ . Returning to $(t,w)$ proves the claim and the postulated continuity extends it to $t=0$ . ∎

#### Theorem B.10 (Viscosity characterization).

Let $\Psi\in\mathfrak{T}$ . Then $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}$ is bounded and continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ , satisfies $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(t,0)=0$ , $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(t,w)=1$ for $w\geq b$ , $\widetilde{V}_{\Psi}(T,\cdot)=\Psi$ , and its restriction to $[0,T]\times[0,b]$ is the unique bounded continuous viscosity solution of (40)–(41).

#### Proof.

Continuity follows from Lemma B.8. At $w=0$ wealth remains zero. At $w\geq b$ , the admissible zero portfolio keeps wealth constant, so $\mathcal{J}=1$ and $\Psi=1$ along the path and the payoff is one. These observations give the boundary values.

The problem (38) is a finite-horizon stochastic control problem with compact control set, state coefficients Lipschitz uniformly over $\Pi_{K}$ , bounded continuous running reward $\lambda\mathcal{J}$ , discount rate $\lambda$ , and bounded continuous terminal reward $\Psi$ . The associated Hamiltonian is

$$ \mathfrak{H}(t,w,r,p,q):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi_{K}}\left\{-\lambda r+wp\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}w^{2}q\,\bm{\pi}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\pi}+\lambda\mathcal{J}(t,w)\right\}. $$

It is finite and continuous. Since the value function is continuous and locally bounded, (Touzi, 2013, Theorem 7.4) gives the viscosity property, and substituting the expression for $\mathfrak{H}$ gives (40). Uniqueness follows by applying Lemma B.9 in both directions. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 5.2.

By Proposition 5.1, the value function agrees with $\widetilde{V}_{\mathcal{T}}$ for $t<T$ . Lemma B.6 gives $\mathcal{T}\in\mathfrak{T}$ , so the result follows from Theorem B.10. ∎

For the committed benchmark, the terminal data are

$$ u(T,w)=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}(w),\quad 0\leq w\leq b,\qquad u(t,0)=0,\quad u(t,b)=1,\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

The main representation result for this problem (Proposition 6.1) follows in the same way, given the reduction in Proposition C.12, which is proved in Section C.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Proposition C.12 gives the stated reduced representation and identifies the committed value with $\widetilde{V}_{\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}}$ for $t<T$ . By Lemma B.6, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}\in\mathfrak{T}$ . The remaining assertions follow from Theorem B.10. ∎

## Appendix C Proofs of Propositions 5.1 and C.12

We first prove the reduction with an arbitrary feasible $\mathcal{G}_{T}$ -measurable terminal decision. The committed case follows by requiring the fixed-deadline goal to be funded whenever affordable.

### C.1 Conventions and Preliminaries

In order to make the conditioning arguments below formal, we take the model on a canonical product space. Consider, for instance, $C([0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^{d})\times[0,\infty)\times[0,b_{R}]\times[0,b_{G}]$ , carrying the Brownian motion, the exponential clock, and the two goal amounts. We then pass to the usual completed, right-continuous filtrations. When regular conditional probabilities appear below, they are taken on the raw countably generated sigma-fields. The resulting conditional identities are then understood almost surely under the completed filtrations. Predictable controls are likewise identified up to $ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ -null sets with raw predictable versions. Importantly, conclusions about the value function remain wholly unchanged by this choice of convention.

For completeness, the full-information filtration used in the main model is the usual augmentation of

$$ \mathcal{G}_{t}^{0}:=\bigcap_{u>t}\left(\mathcal{F}_{u}\vee\sigma(\tau\wedge u)\vee\sigma\!\left(R\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq u\}}\right)\vee\sigma\!\left(G\mathbf{1}_{\{T\leq u\}}\right)\right),\qquad t\geq 0. $$

Then $\tau$ is a $\mathbb{G}$ -stopping time, $R$ is $\mathcal{G}_{\tau}$ -measurable, and $G$ is $\mathcal{G}_{T}$ -measurable. Independence of $(\tau,R,G)$ from $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ implies that $B$ remains a $\mathbb{G}$ -Brownian motion.

We will always work conditionally on $\{\tau>t\}$ and write $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}:=\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\mid\tau>t\,]$ for the conditional expectation with pre-payment wealth started at $w$ at time $t$ . On $\{\tau>t\}$ set $\tau_{t}:=\tau$ . By the memorylessness of the exponential distribution and the independence of $\tau$ from $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)$ , under $\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid\tau>t)$ the residual time $\tau_{t}-t$ is $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ and is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)$ . In particular $\mathbb{P}(\tau_{t}=T\mid\tau>t)=0$ and $\mathbb{P}(\tau_{t}>T\mid\tau>t)=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}$ . For convenience we adopt the same notation for the all-or-nothing post-payment map as in the motivating section: $\Gamma_{a}(x):=x-a\,\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq a\}}$ for $a,x\geq 0$ .

Recall that for $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,u}$ (or $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K}_{t,u}$ ) the pre-payment wealth $\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ is the strong solution of

$$ d\widetilde{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}=\widetilde{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\bigl(\bm{\pi}_{s}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,ds+\bm{\pi}_{s}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dB_{s}\bigr),\qquad\widetilde{W}_{t}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}=w,\quad s\in[t,u]. $$

For $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K}_{t,\infty}$ , let $Y^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ be the pre-decision process obtained by starting from $w$ at time $t$ , following (43) until $\tau_{t}\wedge T$ , applying the update $x\mapsto\Gamma_{R}(x)$ if $\tau_{t}<T$ , and then following (43) until $T$ . Its left limit $Y_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ is determined by $\bm{\pi}$ alone. An admissible pair at $(t,w)$ consists of $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K}_{t,\infty}$ and a $\{0,1\}$ -valued, $\mathcal{G}_{T}$ -measurable variable $d_{T}$ satisfying $d_{T}\in\Theta(Y_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}},G)$ almost surely. For such a pair, the post-payment wealth $\widehat{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}$ is the unique càdlàg $\mathbb{G}$ -adapted solution of

$$ \widehat{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}=w+\int_{t}^{s}\widehat{W}_{r-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}\,\bm{\pi}_{r}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,dr+\int_{t}^{s}\widehat{W}_{r-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}\,\bm{\pi}_{r}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dB_{r}-R\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}\leq s,\ \widehat{W}_{\tau_{t}-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}\geq R\}}-d_{T}G\,\mathbf{1}_{\{T\leq s\}}, $$

$s\geq t$ . Hence $\widehat{W}_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}=Y_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ does not depend on the choice of $d_{T}$ . Well-posedness and nonnegativity follow by solving the diffusion on the stochastic intervals separated by $\tau_{t}$ and $T$ and applying the two feasible jumps.

We remark that for $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\geq 0$ , we may write

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}(s,x) \displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{R}\!\left[\alpha_{R}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq R\}}+\alpha_{D}V^{D}\!\left(s,\Gamma_{R}(x)\right)\right] \displaystyle\phantom{:}=\alpha_{R}F_{R}(x)+\alpha_{D}\!\left[(1-F_{R}(x))V^{D}(s,x)+\int_{0}^{x}V^{D}(s,x-r)\,dF_{R}(r)\right], \displaystyle\mathcal{T}(x) \displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{G}\!\left[\max_{d\in\Theta(x,G)}\{\alpha_{D}d+\alpha_{R}V^{R}(x-dG)\}\right]\phantom{:}=\mathbb{E}_{G}[M(x,G)], $$

where $\mathbb{E}_{R},\mathbb{E}_{G}$ average over the laws of $R$ and $G$ only. Moreover, the following holds for the funding rule $D^{*}$ .

#### Lemma C.1.

The function $D^{*}$ in (22) is Borel, feasible, and attains the maximum $M$ in (23).

#### Proof.

If $x<g$ , only $d=0$ is feasible, while if $x\geq g$ the two candidate values are $\alpha_{R}V^{R}(x)$ and $\alpha_{D}+\alpha_{R}V^{R}(x-g)$ . This proves attainment and (23). The set on which $D^{*}=1$ is

$$ \left\{(x,g):x\geq g,\ \alpha_{D}+\alpha_{R}V^{R}(x-g)\geq\alpha_{R}V^{R}(x)\right\}, $$

which is closed because $V^{R}$ is continuous; hence $D^{*}$ is Borel. ∎

We use throughout the following properties, established in the single-goal analysis: $V^{D}$ and $V^{R}$ take values in $[0,1]$ ; $V^{D}$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ and $V^{R}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ ; and $V^{D}(s,x)=1$ for $x\geq b_{G}$ , $V^{R}(x)=1$ for $x\geq b_{R}$ . With $\sigma_{\lambda}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ , the elementary identity $\mathbb{E}[\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda u}h(u)\,du]=\mathbb{E}[h(\sigma_{\lambda})]$ applied to $h(u)=F_{R}(\widetilde{W}_{u}^{0,x;\bm{\pi}})$ gives the equivalent form

$$ V^{R}(x)=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{0,\infty}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{R}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{\sigma_{\lambda}}^{0,x;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right]. $$

As noted in Lemma B.6, $(s,x)\mapsto\mathcal{J}(s,x)$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ and $x\mapsto\mathcal{T}(x)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ . Hence for $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,T}$ the process $(s,\omega)\mapsto\mathcal{J}(s,\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}_{s})$ is progressively measurable and bounded by $1$ , $\mathcal{T}(\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}_{T})$ is bounded by $1$ , and all expressions are finite.

Finally, for $0\leq t<T$ and $w\geq 0$ , record the main-model value and its reduced counterpart:

$$ V^{R,D}(t,w):=\sup_{(\bm{\pi},d_{T})}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\alpha_{R}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{\tau_{t}-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}\geq R\}}+\alpha_{D}d_{T}\right], $$

$$ \widetilde{V}^{R,D}(t,w):=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,T}}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\mathcal{J}\!\left(s,\widetilde{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)ds+e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\mathcal{T}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right], $$

where the supremum in (48) runs over admissible pairs at $(t,w)$ .

#### C.1.1 Additional Notation

- • For a sigma-field $\mathcal{H}$ on $\Omega$ and a set $A\subseteq\Omega$ , we write $\mathcal{H}|_{A}:=\{H\cap A:H\in\mathcal{H}\}$ for the trace of $\mathcal{H}$ on $A$ . We say that two sigma-fields $\mathcal{H}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ coincide on $A$ if $\mathcal{H}|_{A}=\mathcal{K}|_{A}$ . Equalities of completed sigma-fields below are understood up to completion.

- • For stopping times $S_{1},S_{2}$ , we use the standard stochastic-interval notation $[\![S_{1},S_{2}]\!]:=\{(\omega,u):S_{1}(\omega)\leq u\leq S_{2}(\omega)\}$ , with the analogous meanings for $]\!]S_{1},S_{2}]\!]$ , $[\![S_{1},S_{2}[\![$ , and $]\!]S_{1},S_{2}[\![$ .

- • Let $\mathbb{H}=(\mathcal{H}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be a filtration satisfying the usual conditions with respect to which $B$ is a $d$ -dimensional Brownian motion. If $S$ is an a.s. finite $\mathbb{H}$ -stopping time, we write $B^{S}_{v}:=B_{S+v}-B_{S}$ , $v\geq 0$ , for the Brownian increment process after $S$ . Its augmented natural filtration is denoted by $\mathbb{B}^{S}=(\mathcal{B}^{S}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ . By the strong Markov property, $B^{S}$ is a $d$ -dimensional Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal{H}_{S}$ .

### C.2 Auxiliary Results

Many auxiliary results are needed for the main proof. We provide them here and motivate each.

#### C.2.1 Information Available at the Deadline

Our first lemma shows that if the random-deadline goal has not arrived by $T$ , then the funding decision made at that time can be taken to depend on only the market history and the revealed fixed-goal amount.

#### Lemma C.2.

Set $\mathcal{K}_{T}:=\mathcal{F}_{T}\vee\sigma(G)$ , completed by $\mathbb{P}$ -null sets. If $Y$ is a real-valued $\mathcal{G}_{T}$ -measurable random variable, there is a $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ -measurable $Y^{\prime}$ such that $Y=Y^{\prime}$ a.s. on $\{\tau>T\}$ . Moreover, if $Y$ is $\{0,1\}$ -valued, $Y^{\prime}$ may be chosen to be $\{0,1\}$ -valued. The same statement holds under $\mathbb{P}(\,\cdot\mid\tau>t)$ for every $t<T$ .

#### Proof.

We first show that, up to completion, $\bigcap_{u>T}\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{u}\vee\sigma(G)\bigr)=\mathcal{K}_{T}$ . To this end, fix $u_{m}>T$ with $u_{m}\downarrow T$ and set $\mathcal{A}_{m}:=\mathcal{F}_{u_{m}}\vee\sigma(G)$ and $\mathcal{A}_{\infty}:=\bigcap_{m}\mathcal{A}_{m}$ . For any bounded $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ -measurable $Z$ and bounded Borel $h$ , independence gives that $\mathbb{E}[Zh(G)\mid\mathcal{A}_{m}]=h(G)\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{F}_{u_{m}}]$ . Lévy’s downward theorem and the right continuity of $\mathbb{F}$ therefore give

$$ \mathbb{E}[Zh(G)\mid\mathcal{A}_{\infty}]=h(G)\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}]=h(G)\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]=\mathbb{E}[Zh(G)\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]. $$

A monotone-class argument extends this identity to every bounded $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(G)$ -measurable variable. Applying it to $\mathcal{A}_{\infty}$ -measurable variables yields $\mathcal{A}_{\infty}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{T}$ up to completion. The reverse inclusion is immediate.

Now suppose that the random variable $Y$ in the statement is bounded. On $\{\tau>u_{m}\}$ , the coordinates $\tau\wedge u_{m}$ and $R\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq u_{m}\}}$ are constant. A monotone-class argument on the raw filtration therefore gives uniformly bounded $(\mathcal{F}_{u_{m}}\vee\sigma(G))$ -measurable versions $Y_{m}$ equal to $Y$ on $\{\tau>u_{m}\}$ , outside one common null set. Since the sigma-fields decrease, $Y^{\prime}:=\limsup_{m}Y_{m}$ is measurable with respect to their intersection, which we showed equals $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ . On $\{\tau>T\}$ , we eventually have $u_{m}<\tau$ , so $Y^{\prime}=Y$ . For a general real-valued $Y$ , apply this argument to $\arctan Y$ and invert the transform, extending the inverse arbitrarily off its range. If $Y$ is $\{0,1\}$ -valued, replace $Y^{\prime}$ by $\mathbf{1}_{\{Y^{\prime}\geq 1/2\}}$ . Finally, $\mathbb{P}(\,\cdot\mid\tau>t)\ll\mathbb{P}$ , so the same version gives the conditional statement. ∎

#### C.2.2 Predictable Reductions

The next result is a general result that will be used to justify a reduction in the effective class of controls from $\mathcal{A}_{t,\infty}^{K}$ to $\mathcal{A}_{t,\infty}^{K,\rm pre}$ .

#### Lemma C.3.

Let $\mathbb{H}=(\mathcal{H}_{s})_{s\geq 0}$ satisfy the usual conditions, let $\rho$ be a random time, and let $M$ be a real-valued random variable. Let $\mathbb{G}$ be the progressive enlargement of $\mathbb{H}$ which makes $\rho$ a stopping time and reveals $M$ at $\rho$ , i.e.

$$ \mathcal{G}_{s}=\bigcap_{u>s}\left(\mathcal{H}_{u}\vee\sigma(\rho\wedge u)\vee\sigma(M\mathbf{1}_{\{\rho\leq u\}})\right). $$

Then every (possibly vector-valued) $\mathbb{G}$ -predictable process $Y$ admits an $\mathbb{H}$ -predictable process $Y^{\prime}$ such that $Y=Y^{\prime}$ on $]\!]0,\rho]\!]$ up to evanescence. Consequently, $Y=Y^{\prime}$ $ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. on $[\![0,\rho]\!]$ .

#### Proof.

For the progressive enlargement without $M$ , this is the result of (Aksamit and Jeanblanc, 2017, Proposition 2.11(b)). The case with $M$ follows from the same monotone-class argument. Indeed, $M$ contributes no predictable information on $]\!]0,\rho]\!]$ so every $\mathbb{G}$ -predictable process has an $\mathbb{H}$ -predictable reduction on $]\!]0,\rho]\!]$ , up to evanescence. The stated $ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ conclusion follows because the only difference between $]\!]0,\rho]\!]$ and $[\![0,\rho]\!]$ is the time-zero slice, which is $ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ -null. ∎

As noted above, the next two lemmas use this general result in the context of our problem to argue that we may restrict to pre-arrival controls before goals have arrived.

#### Lemma C.4.

Fix $0\leq t<T$ and work on $\{\tau>t\}$ . For every admissible pair $(\bm{\pi},d_{T})$ there exists $\bm{\pi}^{0}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,T}$ such that

$$ \bm{\pi}_{s}=\bm{\pi}^{0}_{s}\quad\text{for }ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e. }(s,\omega)\text{ with }t\leq s<\tau\wedge T. $$

Consequently, if $\widehat{W}=\widehat{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}$ and $\widetilde{W}=\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}^{0}}$ , then almost surely $\widehat{W}_{s}=\widetilde{W}_{s}$ for $s\in[t,\tau\wedge T)$ , and $\widehat{W}_{\tau-}=\widetilde{W}_{\tau}$ on $\{\tau<T\}$ , $\widehat{W}_{T-}=\widetilde{W}_{T}$ on $\{\tau>T\}$ .

#### Proof.

On $[0,T)$ the component $\sigma(G\mathbf{1}_{\{T\leq u\}})$ in the definition of $\mathbb{G}$ is trivial. Thus, before $T$ , the filtration $\mathbb{G}$ is the progressive enlargement of $\mathbb{F}$ by $\tau$ and the process $R\mathbf{1}_{\tau\leq u}$ . Applying Lemma C.3 to $\bm{\pi}\mathbf{1}_{[t,T)}$ gives an $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable process $\bm{\rho}$ which coincides with $\bm{\pi}$ on $\{(s,\omega):0\leq s<\tau(\omega)\}\cap([t,T)\times\Omega)$ up to evanescence. Let $q_{K}(z):=z\,\mathbf{1}_{\{z\in\Pi_{K}\}}$ for $z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Because $\Pi_{K}$ is closed and $0\in\Pi_{K}$ , $q_{K}$ is a Borel map into $\Pi_{K}$ and is the identity on $\Pi_{K}$ . Thus $\bm{\pi}^{0}:=q_{K}(\bm{\rho})$ is $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable, $\Pi_{K}$ -valued, and still coincides with $\bm{\pi}$ wherever $\bm{\pi}$ already takes values in $\Pi_{K}$ .

Before the first goal resolution no jump in (44) has occurred, so $\widehat{W}$ solves the diffusion equation (43) driven by $\bm{\pi}$ on $[t,\tau\wedge T)$ . The stochastic and drift integrals up to any $s<\tau\wedge T$ depend on the control only through its restriction to $\{t\leq r<s\}$ , where $\bm{\pi}=\bm{\pi}^{0}$ $dr\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. Pathwise uniqueness for (43) gives $\widehat{W}_{s}=\widetilde{W}_{s}$ for $s<\tau\wedge T$ , and the left-limit identities follow from continuity of $\widetilde{W}$ . ∎

#### Lemma C.5.

Let $\mathbb{F}^{G}=(\mathcal{F}_{s}\vee\sigma(G))_{s\geq T}$ and augment it so that it is complete and right-continuous. For every $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K}_{T,\infty}$ there exists an $\mathbb{F}^{G}$ -predictable, $\Pi_{K}$ -valued process $\bm{\pi}^{G}$ on $[T,\infty)$ such that

$$ \bm{\pi}_{s}=\bm{\pi}^{G}_{s}\quad\text{for }ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e. }(s,\omega)\text{ with }T\leq s<\tau. $$

Moreover, for $v\geq 0$ , the process $\bm{\pi}^{G}_{T+v}$ is predictable with respect to $(\mathcal{K}_{T}\vee\mathcal{B}^{T}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ , where $\mathcal{K}_{T}:=\mathcal{F}_{T}\vee\sigma(G)$ and $\mathcal{B}^{T}$ is the augmented natural filtration of $B^{T}=(B_{T+v}-B_{T})_{v\geq 0}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbb{H}=(\mathcal{H}_{s})_{s\geq 0}$ be the initially enlarged Brownian filtration $\mathcal{H}_{s}:=\mathcal{F}_{s}\vee\sigma(G)$ , completed and made right-continuous. On the time region $[T,\infty)$ , the filtration $\mathbb{G}$ is the progressive enlargement of $\mathbb{H}$ by $\tau$ and the process $R\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq u\}}$ . Indeed, $G$ is already contained in $\mathbb{H}$ , while the pair $(\tau,R)$ is revealed only when $\tau$ occurs. Because $G$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ , $B$ remains a Brownian motion in the initially enlarged filtration $\mathbb{H}$ . Applying Lemma C.3 to the $\mathbb{G}$ -predictable process $\bm{\pi}\mathbf{1}_{[T,\infty)}$ gives an $\mathbb{H}$ -predictable process $\bm{\rho}$ which coincides with $\bm{\pi}$ on $[\![0,\tau]\!]\cap([T,\infty)\times\Omega)$ up to evanescence. Restricting to $[T,\infty)$ and applying the Borel retraction $q_{K}(z)=z\mathbf{1}_{\{z\in\Pi_{K}\}}$ used in the preceding lemma yields an $\mathbb{F}^{G}$ -predictable, $\Pi_{K}$ -valued process $\bm{\pi}^{G}$ satisfying the asserted equality for $ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. $(s,\omega)$ with $T\leq s<\tau$ . On $\{\tau\leq T\}$ this set is empty, so nothing else is needed.

Finally, since $\mathcal{F}_{T+v}=\mathcal{F}_{T}\vee\mathcal{B}^{T}_{v}$ up to null sets for Brownian natural filtrations, the initially enlarged filtration satisfies $\mathbb{F}^{G}_{T+v}=\mathcal{K}_{T}\vee\mathcal{B}^{T}_{v}$ up to completion. Hence the process $\bm{\pi}^{G}_{T+v}$ is predictable with respect to $(\mathcal{K}_{T}\vee\mathcal{B}^{T}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ . ∎

#### C.2.3 Representations of Expectations

In our analysis, we will need to simplify expectations in terms of the exponential density. To this end, we supply the following two lemmas.

#### Lemma C.6.

Fix $0\leq t<T$ and work on $\{\tau>t\}$ . Let $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,T}$ and $\widetilde{W}=\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ . For every bounded Borel $f:[t,T]\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[f\!\left(\tau_{t},\widetilde{W}_{\tau_{t}}\right)\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}\right]=\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\,\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[f\!\left(s,\widetilde{W}_{s}\right)\right]ds, $$

and for every bounded Borel $g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[g\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}\right)\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\right]=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\,\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[g\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}\right)\right]. $$

#### Proof.

Under $\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid\tau>t)$ the residual $\eta=\tau_{t}-t$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda u}$ and is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ . Since $\bm{\pi}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable, the path $(\widetilde{W}_{s})_{s\in[t,T]}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{T}$ -measurable and the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto f(s,\widetilde{W}_{s}(\omega))$ is jointly measurable and bounded. By conditioning on $\eta$ , using the density $\lambda e^{-\lambda u}$ , the independence of $\eta$ from $\mathcal{F}_{T}$ , and Fubini’s theorem,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[f(t+\eta,\widetilde{W}_{t+\eta})\mathbf{1}_{\{\eta<T-t\}}\right]=\int_{0}^{T-t}\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[f(t+u,\widetilde{W}_{t+u})]\,du. $$

The change of variables $s=t+u$ gives the first identity. The second follows from $\mathbb{P}(\eta>T-t\mid\tau>t)=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}$ and the independence of $\eta$ from $\widetilde{W}_{T}$ . ∎

#### Lemma C.7.

Fix $0\leq t<T$ and work on $\{\tau>t\}$ . Set $\mathcal{K}_{T}:=\mathcal{F}_{T}\vee\sigma(G)$ and let $\sigma_{\lambda}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ be independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)$ . Let $(\psi(s))_{s\geq T}$ be a bounded process such that $(s,\omega)\mapsto\psi(s,\omega)$ is $\mathcal{B}([T,\infty))\otimes(\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G))$ -measurable, where $\mathcal{B}([T,\infty))$ is the Borel $\sigma$ -field on $[T,\infty)$ . Then, almost surely,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\,\psi(\tau_{t})\,\middle|\,\mathcal{K}_{T}\right]=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\psi(T+\sigma_{\lambda})\,\middle|\,\mathcal{K}_{T}\right]. $$

#### Proof.

On $\{\tau>t\}$ write $\tau_{t}=t+\eta$ with $\eta\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)\supseteq\mathcal{K}_{T}$ . Since $\{\tau>t\}$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)$ , for each $u\geq T-t$ , $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[\psi(t+u)\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]=\mathbb{E}[\psi(t+u)\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]$ . Hence, by the conditional version of Fubini’s theorem,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{t+\eta>T\}}\psi(t+\eta)\,\middle|\,\mathcal{K}_{T}\right]=\int_{T-t}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}[\psi(t+u)\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]\,\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du. $$

Substituting $u=(T-t)+v$ gives $\lambda e^{-\lambda u}=\lambda e^{-\lambda(T-t)}e^{-\lambda v}$ and $t+u=T+v$ . Therefore the right-hand side equals

$$ e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}[\psi(T+v)\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]\,\lambda e^{-\lambda v}\,dv=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\mathbb{E}[\psi(T+\sigma_{\lambda})\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}], $$

where the last equality again uses conditional Fubini and the independence of $\sigma_{\lambda}$ from $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(R,G)$ . ∎

#### C.2.4 Alternative Representation of the Single Goal Value Functions

Next, we will also need an alternative way to interpret the single goal value functions. Let $\beta$ be the coordinate process on $C([0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , let $\mathbb{W}$ be Wiener measure, and let $\mathbb{B}=(\mathcal{B}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ be the usual augmentation of the canonical Brownian filtration. Let $\mathcal{U}^{K}$ be the set of $\Pi_{K}$ -valued $\mathbb{B}$ -predictable processes on this canonical space. Thus each $\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ is a predictable functional of a Brownian increment path. If $W$ is any $d$ -dimensional Brownian motion on any filtered probability space, we write $\bm{\nu}(W)$ for the process obtained by evaluating this functional on the path of $W$ , and let $X^{x;\bm{\nu}}(W)$ solve

$$ dX_{v}=X_{v}\bigl(\bm{\nu}_{v}(W)^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,dv+\bm{\nu}_{v}(W)^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dW_{v}\bigr),\qquad X_{0}=x. $$

Define the following payoffs, with expectation under Wiener measure,

$$ P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{W}}\!\left[F_{G}\!\left(X^{x;\bm{\nu}}_{T-s}(\beta)\right)\right],\qquad P_{R}^{\bm{\nu}}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{W}}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda u}F_{R}\!\left(X^{x;\bm{\nu}}_{u}(\beta)\right)du\right]. $$

Our next result relates these to $V^{D}$ and $V^{R}$ .

#### Lemma C.8.

For all $(s,x)\in[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ , $V^{D}(s,x)=\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)$ and $V^{R}(x)=\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{R}^{\bm{\nu}}(x)$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the fixed-deadline identity. The random deadline identity follows analogously.

Step 1: We first prove the inequality $\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)\leq V^{D}(s,x)$ . Consider the Brownian motion $B^{s}=(B_{s+v}-B_{s})_{v\geq 0}$ . For $\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ the shifted control $\bm{\pi}_{u}:=\bm{\nu}_{u-s}(B^{s})$ , $u\in[s,T]$ , is $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable and $\Pi_{K}$ -valued, so $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{s,T}$ . Moreover, $\widetilde{W}_{T}^{s,x;\bm{\pi}}=X^{x;\bm{\nu}}_{T-s}(B^{s})$ . Since $B^{s}$ has the Wiener law,

$$ P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{G}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{s,x;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right]\leq V^{D}(s,x). $$

Taking the supremum over $\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ gives the desired inequality.

Step 2: Conversely, we can show $V^{D}(s,x)\leq\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)$ . Fix $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{s,T}$ . Let $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}:=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{s})(\omega)$ be a regular conditional probability given $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ , chosen on the underlying raw standard-Borel space (cf. (Kallenberg, 2021, Thm. 8.5)). Since $B^{s}$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ , for $\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. $\omega$ , under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ the process $B^{s}$ is a Brownian motion and every set in $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ has $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ -probability $0$ or $1$ .

By the standing raw-filtration convention, we choose a raw predictable version of $\bm{\pi}$ . On the raw Brownian filtration one has $\mathcal{F}_{s+v}=\mathcal{F}_{s}\vee\mathcal{B}^{s}_{v}$ before completion, so the relative-time process $v\mapsto\bm{\pi}_{s+v}$ is predictable with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_{s}\vee\mathcal{B}^{s}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ . We use the standard predictable factorization fact that, under a conditional law for which $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ is trivial, any $\Pi_{K}$ -valued $(\mathcal{F}_{s}\vee\mathcal{B}^{s}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ -predictable process is equal (up to $dv\otimes d\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ -null sets) to a predictable functional $\bm{\nu}^{\omega}(B^{s})$ for some $\bm{\nu}^{\omega}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ .

Therefore, for $\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. $\omega$ , there exists $\bm{\nu}^{\omega}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ such that

$$ \bm{\pi}_{s+v}=\bm{\nu}^{\omega}_{v}(B^{s})\qquad dv\otimes d\mathbb{P}^{\omega}\text{-a.e. on }[0,T-s]\times\Omega. $$

Under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ , the two controls agree $dv\otimes d\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ -a.e. and are bounded. Hence their drift integrals coincide, and their Itô integrals coincide by the Itô isometry applied to the difference of the two bounded integrands. Pathwise uniqueness for the wealth equation then gives $\widetilde{W}_{T}^{s,x;\bm{\pi}}=X_{T-s}^{x;\bm{\nu}^{\omega}}(B^{s})$ , $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ -a.s. Consequently,

$$ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\omega}}\!\left[F_{G}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{s,x;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right]=P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{\omega}}(s,x)\leq\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x). $$

Taking $\mathbb{P}$ -expectations and using $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\cdot}}[\,\cdot\,]]$ yields $\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{G}\!\left(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{s,x;\bm{\pi}}\right)\right]\leq\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)$ . Taking the supremum over $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{s,T}$ gives $V^{D}(s,x)\leq\sup_{\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}}P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)$ . ∎

We can use these representations to prove two useful estimates.

#### Lemma C.9.

Let $S$ be a finite $\mathbb{G}$ -stopping time and let $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ be a sub- $\sigma$ -algebra, countably generated before completion, such that $S$ is $\mathcal{H}$ -measurable and $B^{S}$ is a Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal{H}$ , and let $X\geq 0$ be $\mathcal{H}$ -measurable. Let $\bm{\pi}$ be a $\Pi_{K}$ -valued process that is predictable with respect to $(\mathcal{H}\vee\mathcal{B}^{S}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ , and let $Z$ solve

$$ dZ_{v}=Z_{v}(\bm{\pi}_{v}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,dv+\bm{\pi}_{v}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dB^{S}_{v}),\qquad Z_{0}=X. $$

Then,

- (i) for every $A\in\mathcal{H}$ such that $S\leq T$ on $A$ , $\mathbf{1}_{A}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{G}(Z_{(T-S)^{+}})\mid\mathcal{H}\right]\leq\mathbf{1}_{A}V^{D}(S\wedge T,X)$ a.s.;

- (ii) if in addition $\sigma_{\lambda}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ is independent of $\mathcal{H}\vee\sigma(B^{S})$ , then $\mathbb{E}\!\left[F_{R}(Z_{\sigma_{\lambda}})\mid\mathcal{H}\right]\leq V^{R}(X)$ a.s.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}:=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H})(\omega)$ be a regular conditional probability given $\mathcal{H}$ (Kallenberg, 2021, Thm. 8.5).

Exactly as in the proof of Lemma C.8, for $\mathbb{P}$ -a.e. $\omega$ : under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ the process $B^{S}$ is a Brownian motion, $S$ and $X$ equal the constants $s:=S(\omega)$ and $x:=X(\omega)$ almost surely, and $\bm{\pi}$ is equal to $\bm{\nu}^{\omega}(B^{S})$ , $dv\otimes d\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ -a.e., for some $\bm{\nu}^{\omega}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ . Since the two controls agree in this sense and are bounded, their drift terms and Itô integrals coincide under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ . Pathwise uniqueness for the wealth SDE gives $Z=X^{x;\bm{\nu}^{\omega}}(B^{S})$ under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ . If $\omega\in A$ , then $s=S(\omega)\leq T$ , so $(T-S)^{+}=T-s$ , and Lemma C.8 gives

$$ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\omega}}\!\left[F_{G}(Z_{(T-S)^{+}})\right]=P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{\omega}}(s,x)\leq V^{D}(s,x). $$

Since $A\in\mathcal{H}$ , this proves part (i) after multiplying by $\mathbf{1}_{A}$ . For (ii), the independence of $\sigma_{\lambda}$ from $\mathcal{H}\vee\sigma(B^{S})$ implies that under $\mathbb{P}^{\omega}$ the variable $\sigma_{\lambda}$ is $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ and independent of $B^{S}$ , whence $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\omega}}[F_{R}(Z_{\sigma_{\lambda}})]=P_{R}^{\bm{\nu}^{\omega}}(x)\leq V^{R}(x)$ by Lemma C.8. ∎

#### C.2.5 Finite Patch Approximation and Predictable Pasting of Controls

Our last auxiliary result builds a finite approximation from $\varepsilon$ -optimal controls.

#### Lemma C.10 (Finite-patch approximation).

For every $\varepsilon>0$ :

- (i) there exist a finite Borel partition $A_{1},\dots,A_{N}$ of $[0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ and controls $\bm{\nu}^{1},\dots,\bm{\nu}^{N}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ such that $P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{i}}(s,x)\geq V^{D}(s,x)-\varepsilon$ whenever $(s,x)\in A_{i}$ ;

- (ii) there exist a finite Borel partition $B_{1},\dots,B_{M}$ of $[0,b_{R}]$ and controls $\bm{\zeta}^{1},\dots,\bm{\zeta}^{M}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ such that $P_{R}^{\bm{\zeta}^{j}}(y)\geq V^{R}(y)-\varepsilon$ whenever $y\in B_{j}$ .

For $x\geq b_{G}$ in (i) or $y\geq b_{R}$ in (ii), the zero control is exactly optimal, attaining the value $1$ .

#### Proof.

We first record two continuity facts. By scaling, the solution of (43) satisfies $X^{x;\bm{\nu}}_{v}(\beta)=x\,\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\nu}}_{v}$ with $\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\nu}}_{v}:=\exp\!\bigl(\int_{0}^{v}(\bm{\nu}_{r}^{\top}\bm{\theta}-\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{\nu}_{r}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\nu}_{r})\,dr+\int_{0}^{v}\bm{\nu}_{r}^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,d\beta_{r}\bigr)$ , which has continuous paths and does not depend on $x$ . Hence, for fixed $\bm{\nu}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ , $(s,x)\mapsto x\,\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\nu}}_{T-s}$ is a.s. jointly continuous, and since $F_{G}\in[0,1]$ is continuous, bounded convergence gives that $(s,x)\mapsto P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{W}}[F_{G}(x\,\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\nu}}_{T-s})]$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times[0,\infty)$ . Likewise, for fixed $\bm{\zeta}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ and $x\to x^{\prime}$ , $F_{R}(x\,\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\zeta}}_{u})\to F_{R}(x^{\prime}\,\mathcal{E}^{\bm{\zeta}}_{u})$ for every $(u,\omega)$ by continuity of $F_{R}$ . Since $F_{R}\in[0,1]$ dominated convergence on $\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du\otimes d\mathbb{W}$ shows $x\mapsto P_{R}^{\bm{\zeta}}(x)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ .

For (i), fix $\varepsilon>0$ . For each $(s,x)\in[0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ , Lemma C.8 provides $\bm{\nu}^{s,x}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ with $P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{s,x}}(s,x)\geq V^{D}(s,x)-\varepsilon/3$ . The function $(s^{\prime},x^{\prime})\mapsto V^{D}(s^{\prime},x^{\prime})-P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{s,x}}(s^{\prime},x^{\prime})$ is continuous and is $\leq\varepsilon/3$ at $(s,x)$ , so it is $<\varepsilon$ on a relatively open neighborhood $U_{s,x}$ of $(s,x)$ . Therefore, on $U_{s,x}$ , $P_{D}^{\bm{\nu}^{s,x}}\geq V^{D}-\varepsilon$ . These neighborhoods cover the compact set $[0,T]\times[0,b_{G}]$ and so we can extract a finite subcover $U_{s_{1},x_{1}},\dots,U_{s_{N},x_{N}}$ . From this we can construct a disjoint cover so that we arrive at a Borel partition $A_{1},\dots,A_{N}$ with $A_{i}\subseteq U_{s_{i},x_{i}}$ and controls $\bm{\nu}^{i}:=\bm{\nu}^{s_{i},x_{i}}$ . Part (ii) is identical on the compact interval $[0,b_{R}]$ . Finally, under the zero control wealth is constant, so if $x\geq b_{G}$ then $F_{G}(x)=1=V^{D}(s,x)$ and if $y\geq b_{R}$ then $F_{R}(y)=1=V^{R}(y)$ . ∎

#### Remark C.11.

In the main proof of Proposition 5.1 we use the following standard predictable-pasting fact. Let $S$ be a $\mathbb{G}$ -stopping time, let $C_{1},\dots,C_{m}$ be a finite $\mathcal{G}_{S}$ -measurable partition, and let $\bm{\nu}^{1},\dots,\bm{\nu}^{m}\in\mathcal{U}^{K}$ . Then the process

$$ \Pi_{r}:=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{C_{k}}\,\bm{\nu}^{k}_{(r-S)^{+}}(B^{S})\,\mathbf{1}_{\{S<r\}},\qquad r\geq 0, $$

is $\mathbb{G}$ -predictable and $\Pi_{K}$ -valued. More generally, finite concatenations of such shifted controls at $\mathbb{G}$ -stopping times remain admissible.

### C.3 Main Proof

We are now ready to complete the proof of the proposition.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.1.

Fix $(t,w)$ , work under $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}$ , and let $(\bm{\pi},d_{T})$ be an admissible pair. Write

$$ P:=\alpha_{R}I_{R}+\alpha_{D}d_{T},\qquad I_{R}:=\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{\tau_{t}-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}\geq R\}},\qquad\widehat{W}:=\widehat{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi},d_{T}}. $$

Since $\mathbb{P}(\tau_{t}=T\mid\tau>t)=0$ , split the payoff over $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ and $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ .

Step 1 (upper bound). Let $\bm{\pi}^{0}$ be the pre-deadline reduction of Lemma C.4, and write $\widetilde{W}:=\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}^{0}}$ . On $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ , $\widehat{W}_{\tau_{t}-}=\widetilde{W}_{\tau_{t}}$ and the post-payment wealth is $\Gamma_{R}(\widetilde{W}_{\tau_{t}})$ . Feasibility gives $d_{T}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{T-}\geq G\}}$ . On the stochastic interval $]\!]\tau_{t},T[\![$ , no further non-Brownian information is revealed. More precisely, for each $v\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}+v}\big|_{\{\tau_{t}+v<T\}}=\bigl(\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}\vee\mathcal{B}^{\tau_{t}}_{v}\bigr)\big|_{\{\tau_{t}+v<T\}}, $$

up to completion. A standard predictable-factorization argument shows that the shifted continuation control $\bm{\pi}^{\tau_{t}}_{v}:=\bm{\pi}_{\tau_{t}+v}\mathbf{1}_{\{0<v<T-\tau_{t}\}}$ , $v\geq 0$ , has a $\Pi_{K}$ -valued version that is predictable with respect to $(\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}\vee\mathcal{B}^{\tau_{t}}_{v})_{v\geq 0}$ .

Consequently, on $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ , the continuation wealth $\widehat{W}_{T-}$ is measurable with respect to the trace of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}\vee\sigma(\tau,R)$ , which also contains the trace of $\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}$ . Since $G$ is independent of this sigma-field under $\mathbb{P}(\,\cdot\mid\tau>t)$ , averaging over $G$ and applying Lemma C.9(i) therefore gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[d_{T}\mid\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}]\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}} \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{T-}\geq G\}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}]\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[F_{G}(\widehat{W}_{T-})\mid\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}]\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}\leq V^{D}\!\left(\tau_{t},\Gamma_{R}(\widetilde{W}_{\tau_{t}})\right)\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}. $$

Adding the random-goal reward, averaging over $R$ , and applying Lemma C.6 yields

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}[P\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}]\leq\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[\mathcal{J}(s,\widetilde{W}_{s})]\,ds. $$

On $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ , $\widehat{W}_{T-}=\widetilde{W}_{T}$ . By Lemma C.2, choose a $\{0,1\}$ -valued $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ -measurable $d_{T}^{\prime}$ equal to $d_{T}$ on this event and set $\bar{d}:=d_{T}^{\prime}\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{W}_{T}\geq G\}}$ and $X:=\widetilde{W}_{T}-\bar{d}G$ . Then $\bar{d}\in\Theta(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ everywhere, $\bar{d}=d_{T}$ on $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ , and $X$ is nonnegative and $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ -measurable. Lemma C.5 produces a $\mathbb{F}^{G}$ -predictable continuation control agreeing with $\bm{\pi}$ before $\tau_{t}$ . Let $Z$ denote its relative-time wealth process:

$$ dZ_{v}=Z_{v}\Bigl((\bm{\pi}^{G}_{T+v})^{\top}\bm{\theta}\,dv+(\bm{\pi}^{G}_{T+v})^{\top}\bm{\sigma}\,dB^{T}_{v}\Bigr),\qquad Z_{0}=X. $$

Pathwise uniqueness gives $\widehat{W}_{\tau_{t}-}=Z_{\tau_{t}-T}$ on $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ . The process $\psi(s):=\mathbf{1}_{\{Z_{s-T}\geq R\}}$ , $s\geq T$ , is bounded and jointly measurable in the sense of Lemma C.7. Hence Lemma C.7, independence of $R$ , and Lemma C.9(ii) give $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[I_{R}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]\leq e^{-\lambda(T-t)}V^{R}(X)$ . The fixed-goal term satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[d_{T}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\bar{d}$ . Since $\bar{d}\in\Theta(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ , Lemma C.1 implies $\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[P\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]\leq e^{-\lambda(T-t)}M(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ . Averaging over $G$ therefore gives

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}[P\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}]\leq e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[\mathcal{T}(\widetilde{W}_{T})]. $$

Combining (50) and (51), then taking the supremum over admissible pairs, proves $V^{R,D}\leq\widetilde{V}^{R,D}$ .

Step 2 (lower bound). Fix $\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,\mathrm{pre}}_{t,T}$ , set $\widetilde{W}:=\widetilde{W}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}$ , fix $\varepsilon>0$ , and take the finite patches of Lemma C.10. Construct a full strategy $\bm{\pi}^{\varepsilon}$ and decision $d_{T}^{\varepsilon}$ as follows. Use $\bm{\pi}$ before $\tau_{t}\wedge T$ . On $\{\tau_{t}=s<T\}$ , put $X_{s}:=\Gamma_{R}(\widetilde{W}_{s})$ and, on $]\!]s,T]\!]$ , use the zero control when $X_{s}\geq b_{G}$ , and otherwise the shifted control $\bm{\nu}^{i}(B^{\tau_{t}})$ selected by $(s,X_{s})\in A_{i}$ . At $T$ set $d_{T}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{T-}\geq G\}}$ on $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ , and use the zero control after $T$ on this branch. On $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ , set $d_{T}^{\varepsilon}:=D^{*}(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ , $Y_{T}:=\widetilde{W}_{T}-d_{T}^{\varepsilon}G$ , and, on $]\!]T,\tau_{t}]\!]$ , use the zero control when $Y_{T}\geq b_{R}$ , and otherwise the shifted control $\bm{\zeta}^{j}(B^{T})$ selected by $Y_{T}\in B_{j}$ . Use the zero control after $\tau_{t}$ . Define the pair arbitrarily and feasibly on the null event $\{\tau_{t}=T\}$ .

The switching events are measurable at the corresponding stopping times. Remark C.11 therefore makes $\bm{\pi}^{\varepsilon}$ admissible. The decision is $\mathcal{G}_{T}$ -measurable because $D^{*}$ is Borel, and is feasible because $D^{*}(x,g)\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq g\}}$ . Thus $(\bm{\pi}^{\varepsilon},d_{T}^{\varepsilon})$ is an admissible pair. In the remainder of this step, let $P$ and $I_{R}$ denote the payoff and random-goal indicator generated by this constructed pair.

On $\{\tau_{t}=s<T\}$ , conditioning at $\tau_{t}$ and integrating the independent Brownian increments gives

$$ \mathbb{E}[d_{T}^{\varepsilon}\mid\mathcal{G}_{\tau_{t}}]\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}\geq\left(V^{D}\!\left(\tau_{t},\Gamma_{R}(\widetilde{W}_{\tau_{t}})\right)-\varepsilon\right)\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}, $$

where there is no approximation loss when $X_{s}\geq b_{G}$ . Averaging over $R$ and using Lemma C.6 gives

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}[P\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}<T\}}]\geq\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[\mathcal{J}(s,\widetilde{W}_{s})]\,ds-\alpha_{D}\varepsilon(1-e^{-\lambda(T-t)}). $$

On $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ , the post-decision wealth is $Y_{T}=\widetilde{W}_{T}-D^{*}(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)G$ . Applying Lemma C.7 and the selected random-goal patch conditionally on $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ gives

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}[I_{R}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}\mid\mathcal{K}_{T}]\geq e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\bigl(V^{R}(Y_{T})-\varepsilon\bigr), $$

again with no approximation loss when $Y_{T}\geq b_{R}$ . The fixed-goal term is $e^{-\lambda(T-t)}D^{*}(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ conditionally on $\mathcal{K}_{T}$ . Since $D^{*}$ attains $M$ , averaging over $G$ yields

$$ \mathbb{E}_{t,w}[P\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{t}>T\}}]\geq e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}[\mathcal{T}(\widetilde{W}_{T})]-\alpha_{R}\varepsilon e^{-\lambda(T-t)}. $$

Adding (52) and (53), and using $C_{t,T}:=\alpha_{D}(1-e^{-\lambda(T-t)})+\alpha_{R}e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\leq 1$ , shows that the reduced payoff generated by $\bm{\pi}$ is at most $V^{R,D}(t,w)+\varepsilon C_{t,T}$ . Let $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ and take the supremum over pre-deadline controls to obtain the reverse inequality. This proves Proposition 5.1. ∎

We note that the construction in Step 2 of the proof demonstrates that the value is unchanged when every affordable fixed-deadline goal is funded on $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ and the decision $D^{*}(Y_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}},G)$ is used on $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ .

#### Proposition C.12.

For every $(t,w)\in[0,T)\times[0,\infty)$ ,

$$ V_{\mathrm{commit}}^{R,D}(t,w)=\sup_{\bm{\pi}\in\mathcal{A}^{K,{\rm pre}}_{t,T}}\mathbb{E}_{t,w}\!\left[\int_{t}^{T}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s-t)}\mathcal{J}\bigl(s,\widetilde{W}_{s}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\bigr)\,ds+e^{-\lambda(T-t)}\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}\bigl(\widetilde{W}_{T}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\bigr)\right]. $$

#### Proof of Proposition C.12.

Define $d_{T}^{\rm commit}(\bm{\pi}):=\mathbf{1}_{\{Y_{T-}^{t,w;\bm{\pi}}\geq G\}}$ and fix $d_{T}=d_{T}^{\rm commit}(\bm{\pi})$ . On $\{\tau_{t}<T\}$ , the inequality $d_{T}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{W}_{T-}\geq G\}}$ in the preceding proof is an equality, so the contribution $\mathcal{J}$ is unchanged. On $\{\tau_{t}>T\}$ , we have $\bar{d}=\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{W}_{T}\geq G\}}$ . The post-decision wealth is $\Gamma_{G}(\widetilde{W}_{T})$ , and $M(\widetilde{W}_{T},G)$ is replaced by $\alpha_{D}\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{W}_{T}\geq G\}}+\alpha_{R}V^{R}(\Gamma_{G}(\widetilde{W}_{T}))$ . Averaging over $G$ gives $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{commit}}$ . In the lower bound, use the same finite patches and the prescribed decision instead of $D^{*}$ . The estimates (52)–(53) are unchanged except for the same replacement of the terminal operator. Taking suprema gives (54), which proves the proposition. ∎

We show here that the qualitative findings of the growth crowding-out effect and the deadline pressure effect from Section 7.4 are robust to variations in goal dispersion, the fixed-goal amount, the random-goal specification, and college saving horizons.

Figures 14 and 15 vary the dispersion $\sigma_{G}$ of the fixed-deadline goal distribution across retirement and college calibrations respectively. ### D.2 Additional Robustness of the Value-of-Flexibility Results

In this section, we complement the analysis in Section 7.5 by showing the sensitivity of the ex ante and terminal option values to the precautionary-goal arrival intensity $\lambda$ , the parameter that most directly governs the urgency of the random-deadline goal. Unless otherwise indicated, all numerical results in this section use the setup of Section 7.5 in the main manuscript: $(\alpha_{D},\alpha_{R})=(0.10,0.90)$ , $T=18$ , $\lambda=0.20$ , a truncated-lognormal accumulation goal with median $G_{0}=\$124{,}000$ and $\sigma_{G}=0.5$ , and the near-degenerate precautionary-goal distribution centered at $R_{0}=\$29{,}837.40$ . Under the main manuscript’s baseline equal weights, flexibility has no value by Proposition 6.2. We discuss sensitivity to accumulation-goal priority per dollar $\alpha_{D}/G_{0}$ in Section 7.5. In Section D.2.2, we report an additional priority experiment that varies $\alpha_{D}$ with $G_{0}$ fixed, together with sensitivity of the ex ante option value to the deterministic deadline $T$ .

#### D.2.1 Arrival-Intensity Sensitivity

Figures 19 and 20 show the effect of varying $\lambda$ .
